output.title: When a retainer turns into open-ended work
output.body:
If you run a small business, the quiet cost of an open-ended retainer is not just the invoice. It is the way the work can drift: one more request, one more follow-up, one more exception that nobody planned for.

That is the point where I would make the decision concrete. Pick one recurring workflow — repeated customer questions, neglected sales leads, or manual invoice/data work — and ask whether it deserves a bounded automation pilot instead of an open-ended arrangement.

For a representative owner-operator, that kind of work can add up to about 8–10 hours a week. That is not a market statistic; it is the sort of routine drag that tells you the workflow is worth looking at.

Bareni’s normal sequence is simple: a free 30-minute diagnostic, then a one-page pilot proposal, then a fixed-price working MVP or pilot. The scope is defined up front. The timings are intended as scopes, not guarantees. After that, you can decide whether expansion or an optional retainer makes sense.

I would not push AI into legal, medical, financial-compliance, bulk cold email, or scan-heavy OCR work. Money movement stays under human approval.

The next step is manual: write down the one workflow, the hours it consumes now, and the one outcome that would justify a pilot. Then decide whether the work is better handled as a bounded build or kept inside a retainer.
